findings.title: Parallel index init shares err and can ignore build failures
findings.body: searchSupport.init starts one errgroup goroutine per namespace, but every goroutine assigns the build result to the single outer err variable and returns that same variable. BuildIndex used to hold its cache mutex for the whole build, so those goroutines mostly ran one at a time; after the lock was narrowed they actually run in parallel and the unsynchronized err writes race. A goroutine whose build failed can observe nil after another goroutine's success overwrites err, return nil, and let errgroup.Wait succeed, so the server starts with that namespace missing from the index. The reverse also happens: a successful goroutine can return another goroutine's error and fail startup incorrectly. totalBatchesIndexed is incremented from the same goroutines without synchronization. Each goroutine needs its own error variable.

findings.title: Narrowed BuildIndex lock races same-key builds and clobbers the cache
findings.body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The mutex is now taken only for b.cache[key] = idx. getOrCreateIndex in search.go is still check-then-build with no per-key lock (the TODO above it says so), so two searches, or a search and a watch event, for a namespace that was not prebuilt can both miss the cache and build at once. File-backed builds then call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently; that races inside bleve, and the loser fails with path-already-exists even though an index was created. Memory builds both succeed and the later cache write replaces the earlier index without closing it, so watch updates applied to the replaced index disappear from later searches and the orphaned index leaks. In-flight builds need to be deduplicated per NamespacedResource, and the cache insert must keep an existing entry instead of overwriting it.

findings.title: Index watch starts at the latest RV and drops writes made during the build
findings.body: build returns the resource version observed while listing a namespace, and the comment on that return says watchers must apply every event since that version. init discards the returned version and then calls WatchWriteEvents, which samples the latest resource version at subscription time and only delivers newer rows. Creates, updates, and deletes that commit after a namespace was listed and before that subscription — expected when another HA replica writes during the long startup index build — are neither in the listed snapshot nor replayed. Updated documents stay stale in the search index, and deletes from that window remain searchable until a full rebuild. Namespaces are listed concurrently, so each list has its own version; the watch cursor has to be the earliest of those list versions, not the global maximum after every build finishes.

findings.title: File indexes cannot be reopened, so eager init fails every restart
findings.body: File-backed indexes are created with bleve.New on a stable path (Root/namespace/resource.group). bleve.New fails if that directory already exists, and this code never calls bleve.Open or deletes a leftover directory. If the builder fails, BuildIndex returns without closing the index or removing the partial directory. After the first successful file-backed build, or after a failed build that created the directory, the next process calls BuildIndex again, bleve.New fails, and NewResourceServer now aborts Init and refuses to construct the server. FileThreshold's zero value is 0, so any namespace with a positive count uses disk unless the caller sets a higher threshold. Startup must reopen or replace an existing directory, and error paths must delete partial indexes, or a normal restart cannot bring the storage server up.

findings.title: Init failure returns nil without rolling back partial startup
findings.body: NewResourceServer now calls Init and, on error, returns nil without calling the cancel func created above, lifecycle.Stop, or closing the blob bucket opened earlier in the constructor. If lifecycle.Init already opened the SQL database, those connections leak because the caller has no server value on which to call Stop. If search indexing succeeded and only the later watcher setup failed, search.init has already started a watch goroutine on context.Background that nothing will stop. Indexes already published into the caller-owned SearchBackend stay cached, so a retry that reuses that backend treats them as complete and skips rebuilding. Failure needs to stop lifecycle hooks, cancel background work, and drop partial indexes before returning the error.

findings.title: Search watch loop ignores shutdown and panics when the event channel closes
findings.body: After indexing, init starts a goroutine that reads WatchWriteEvents in a bare for loop and does not check the receive ok value. The watch context is context.Background, not the server context cancelled by Stop, so server shutdown does not stop the loop. The SQL poller closes that channel when the backend stops; the next receive yields a nil event, and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type and panics, crashing the process during shutdown. If the backend is never stopped, the goroutine and poller leak for the rest of the process. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer, so this goroutine is created for every search-enabled server, including ones that are constructed and shut down without serving a request. The loop should use the server lifetime context and exit when the channel closes.
